paras: The threatened lynching of Alexander Ellison took place at Woodland Mills, Obion County, Tennessee, in early August 1880, after Ellison, a Black man, shot a white man named Harry Crenshaw on the night of Sunday, August 1. Wire dispatches said a crowd was pursuing Ellison to lynch him and that he was expected to be lynched after his arrest, and the story ran in papers from Washington to Dallas. A nearby Kentucky paper reported a week later that Ellison was in jail at Troy and that a report of his hanging was untrue.

Woodland Mills lay about six miles from Union City. According to a Nashville Banner special, a party of Black people was swearing and quarreling in front of the house of Crenshaw, "a well-known citizen," on Sunday night, and Crenshaw went out and ordered them to hush.

Hot words followed, and in the wire versions Crenshaw fired at the group first. Ellison, one of the party, answered with a double-barreled shotgun, emptying both barrels into Crenshaw's breast and stomach, and Crenshaw was carried into his house. The earliest telegrams said Crenshaw had been mortally wounded and that "A crowd is pursuing Elison and will lynch him if caught."

Ellison fled to Union City, where he was arrested on the morning of August 2 and taken back to Woodland Mills. A Nashville special relayed through New York added that "it is thought he will be lynched to-night" and called Ellison "generally regarded as a bad character." By August 6 he had been taken to the jail at Troy.

On August 13 the Hickman Courier reported that Ellison, whom it now called the man "who killed Harry Crenshaw," was in jail at Troy and that "The report that he was taken from the jail and hung was not true." The same paper said white sentiment was divided, with some white citizens holding that Ellison was "not as censurable as first reports had it." No report of Crenshaw's death, an inquest, an indictment or a trial was found.

The episode reached the press through several separate Nashville dispatches, which agreed that Crenshaw fired first and differed mainly on whether Ellison was still at large. Headlines put race in front: the Evening Star ran "A Negro Who Shot a White Man in Danger of Lynching," the Chicago Tribune "Shot by a Negro," and the Dallas Daily Herald "White Man Killed by a Negro." The National Republican headed its second printing "Threatened Lynching in Tennessee," and the Wilmington Daily Gazette set the item under "Republican Negroes Killing Colored Democrats," a heading drawn from an unrelated Kentucky story in the same paragraph.

Reprints carried the expected lynching as settled news, one New Hampshire summary closing with "Lynching is expected," and the story was still being reprinted in South Carolina on August 12. The Hickman Courier, published near the scene, at first described Crenshaw as "an exemplary citizen" and Ellison as drunk and insulting, but a week later recorded the divided white opinion and denied the hanging rumor. No coverage in the Black press was found.

The Hickman Courier gave the only version in which Ellison fired first: it said a drunken Ellison dared Crenshaw to come out of his yard, and that when Crenshaw took his gun and started across the fence with two young white men, Ellison put 25 shot into his legs and abdomen. Crenshaw's fate was also reported differently: an Alexandria Gazette condensation said he was killed instantly and that his own shot had killed one of the Black party, while the Hickman Courier said on August 6 that he "yet survives" and a week later referred to him as killed.

reader.title: Threatened lynching of Alexander Ellison
bases: After a Black man shot a white man, wire reports said a crowd was pursuing him to lynch him and that he was expected to be lynched after his arrest (A2, A3, A4), but a later local report said a story of his being hanged was untrue and he was in jail (A15): a threatened lynching.

Ellison was threatened by a pursuing crowd (A1, A2) and expected to be lynched (A3, A4), but the Hickman Courier reported a week later that he was in jail at Troy and that the report of his hanging 'was not true' (A15); no one was killed by a mob.

Independent dispatches (the Nashville Banner special in A5, the Commercial's Nashville dispatch in A4, the New York-relayed special in A3) and the nearby Hickman Courier (A13, A15) agree that Ellison shot Crenshaw at Woodland Mills, fled, was arrested and was threatened with lynching or held in jail.

accounts.label: Nashville wire specials (Banner and others)
accounts.gist: A party of Black people was cursing and quarreling in front of Crenshaw's house; he ordered them to stop, words followed, and Crenshaw fired into the group, after which Ellison returned fire with a double-barreled shotgun.

accounts.label: Early brief telegrams
accounts.gist: Crenshaw was shot and mortally wounded by Elison, and a crowd was pursuing Elison and would lynch him if caught; no mention of Crenshaw firing.

accounts.label: Alexandria Gazette condensation
accounts.gist: Crenshaw shot into the crowd and killed one of its members, and the party's return fire killed Crenshaw instantly.

accounts.label: Hickman Courier (nearby local paper)
accounts.gist: A drunken Elison defied Crenshaw to come out of his yard; Crenshaw took his gun and, with two young white men, started across the fence, and Elison fired first, putting 25 shot into his legs and abdomen.

framing.detail: The wire versions stated that Crenshaw fired first and reported the expected lynching flatly, while the Evening Star's headline 'A Negro Who Shot a White Man in Danger of Lynching' and the remark that Ellison was 'generally regarded as a bad character' leaned against him.
The Hickman Courier first called Crenshaw 'an exemplary citizen' and Elison drunk and insulting, then a week later reported that some white citizens thought him less censurable than first reported.
Papers from Washington to Dallas and New Hampshire reprinted the dispatches under headlines such as 'Threatened Lynching in Tennessee', 'Fatal Affrays' and 'White Man Killed by a Negro'.
The Wilmington Daily Gazette placed the dispatch under the partisan headline 'Republican Negroes Killing Colored Democrats', though the item gave no political motive.
